opus-5.5.text:
Well, the key insight is that in TensorLogic, structure and weights aren't really separate things. A logical rule is a tensor equation: you join some tensors, project out some indices, and maybe apply a nonlinearity. If you make those tensors learnable, then which connections matter becomes a matter of which weights end up nonzero or significant. Structure learning becomes weight learning.

Think about how inductive logic programming traditionally worked. You'd search a combinatorial space of candidate rules, adding a literal here, removing one there, scoring each candidate. That's expensive and brittle. In TensorLogic you can instead write a very general rule, say a relation defined as a combination of other relations over some set of variables, with a weight tensor that says how much each piece contributes. Then you learn by gradient descent. If a weight goes to zero, that part of the rule effectively disappears. If it becomes large, you've discovered a dependency. You can read the learned rule back off the weights.

This also works the other way. A neural network is already a set of tensor equations, so a multilayer perceptron or a transformer can be written as a handful of TensorLogic rules. What we call "architecture" is just a particular sparsity pattern and sharing of weights. So learning structure and learning parameters live in one space, and you can move continuously between a dense, neural-looking model and a sparse, symbolic-looking one.

The part I find most exciting is that this gives you something like predicate invention for free. You can posit intermediate tensors with no predefined meaning, embeddings or hidden relations, and the learning process decides what they should represent. Then, if you want something interpretable, you can push toward sparsity or turn down the temperature so the soft reasoning becomes closer to hard logical deduction, and you recover crisp rules.

It isn't magic. You still choose a space of possible rules, the variables, the order of the tensors, and that's an inductive bias. Real structure discovery in very large spaces is still hard, and optimization can get stuck. But it turns what used to be a discrete search problem into a continuous one, which is what deep learning is good at, while keeping the transparency and compositionality of logic. To me that's what the unification of neural and symbolic AI should look like: not two systems bolted together, but one language where the distinction dissolves.

r001.rationale: The response says a general TensorLogic rule uses learnable weights to determine which dependencies remain, with zero weights removing parts of the rule; this selects structure from what the equation can represent.

r002.rationale: It describes neural networks as TensorLogic rules and says architecture is a pattern of weight sparsity and sharing, with structure and parameter learning in one space.

r003.rationale: It does not identify TensorLogic structure learning as extending propositional rule learning to first-order logic.

r004.rationale: It mentions sparsity and crisp rules, but does not say users can choose which learned structural elements to discretize and which to retain as weights.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, this is one of the things I find most beautiful about Tensor Logic, and it falls out almost for free once you take the core idea seriously. The core idea is that a logical rule and an Einstein summation are the same thing. A Datalog rule like "grandparent of X and Z if parent of X and Y and parent of Y and Z" is literally a tensor contraction: you take the parent tensor, multiply it with itself along the shared index Y, and you project out. The join is the product, the projection is the sum. So a rule is a tensor equation, and a program is a set of tensor equations.

Now, once you're in that world, structure learning stops being this separate, combinatorial, discrete search problem that it's been in inductive logic programming for thirty years. In ILP you have to enumerate candidate clauses, add a literal, remove a literal, score it, backtrack. It's painful and it doesn't scale. In Tensor Logic, the structure is just which entries of which tensors are nonzero. If I have a tensor that could in principle connect any predicate to any other predicate through any set of shared indices, and I initialize it densely or with some prior, then gradient descent on the weights is doing structure learning. A weight going to zero is a literal being dropped from a rule. A weight that stays large is a literal being kept. A whole rule disappears when its weights all vanish. So the space of programs is embedded in a continuous space of tensors, and you search it with the same backpropagation that trains everything else.

The other thing that happens, and I think this is underappreciated, is that the embeddings do the generalization for you. Because objects are vectors rather than atoms, the "structure" you learn isn't just symbolic templates over fixed constants. The same rule applies to things that are close in embedding space, so you get soft, analogical structure. In the limit where the temperature goes to zero, you recover crisp logic and the learned structure is a real, readable set of rules you can inspect and verify. Turn the temperature up and you have something more like a neural network that reasons approximately. And you can move continuously between the two. That's the point. Neural nets and symbolic AI were never really different things; the dichotomy was an artifact of how we wrote them down.

I should be honest about the hard part, though. The naive version where every tensor is dense over every possible index is exponential, so you need sparsity, and you need priors on which contractions are even allowed, and getting the optimization to actually find clean, sparse structure rather than a smeared-out mess is where the real engineering is. Weight learning with an L1-style pressure helps, the symbolic prior in the equations themselves helps enormously because you're not starting from a blank slate, and I think there's a lot of room for better methods there. But the conceptual shift is what matters: structure learning is weight learning, if you choose the right representation. And I think that representation is tensor logic.

r001.rationale: The response says gradient descent on tensor weights performs structure learning: weights going to zero drop literals, while surviving weights keep them, selecting a program from the structures the tensors can represent.

r002.rationale: It says TensorLogic makes structure learning into weight learning, but does not explain ordinary neural-network weight learning as learning the structure of logical rules.

r003.rationale: It gives a first-order Datalog example, but does not identify TensorLogic's structure learning as extending propositional rule learning to first-order logic.

r004.rationale: It describes moving between crisp logic and approximate neural reasoning via temperature, but does not state that one can selectively discretize some learned structural elements while retaining others as weights.

astra-6.text:
The key idea is that you can represent choices about structure as choices about weights. Imagine starting with a network containing all the connections you might want. A weight of zero effectively removes a connection; a nonzero weight keeps it. So learning the weights can also mean learning which connections exist.

In TensorLogic, you can apply that idea to candidate logical rules or ways of composing tensor operations. Instead of searching separately over discrete structures, you embed those alternatives in a parameterized computation and learn which ones are useful.

But there’s an important qualification: ordinary weight learning doesn’t automatically give you a clean, discrete structure. You generally need some pressure toward sparsity, or a mechanism for selecting alternatives. And the space of structures you can discover is determined by what your representation makes available. So the interesting claim is that structure learning and parameter learning can be brought into the same framework, rather than treated as two completely separate problems.

r001.rationale: The response says TensorLogic embeds candidate rules or tensor-operation compositions in a parameterized computation and learns which alternatives are useful, selecting structure from what the representation makes available.

r002.rationale: It says ordinary network weight learning can select connections, but does not interpret that as learning the structure of a set of logical rules.

r003.rationale: It does not mention extending propositional rule learning to first-order logic.

r004.rationale: It mentions sparsity or selection mechanisms, but does not say users can choose which learned structural elements to discretize and which to retain as weights.

sol-6.1.text:
The key idea is that you can represent a choice of structure as a choice of weights. Suppose you have a very general network containing all the connections you might want. Learning a particular architecture then amounts to setting some of those weights to zero and letting others be nonzero. A zero weight effectively removes a connection.

In TensorLogic, you can apply that idea to the logical structure as well. You can have candidate rules, or candidate ways of combining predicates, and learn which ones matter through their weights. So something that looks like a discrete search over structures can, in principle, become a continuous optimization problem.

Now, there’s an important qualification: you still have to specify the space of possibilities. Weight learning doesn’t magically invent anything outside that space. And if you want a compact, interpretable structure, you need something that encourages sparsity or otherwise penalizes complexity. But the attraction is that you can use the machinery of gradient-based learning to do work that would traditionally require a separate structure-learning algorithm.

r001.rationale: It explains that a general network can select a particular architecture by setting some connection weights to zero, and applies the same idea to TensorLogic’s candidate rules and predicate combinations.

r002.rationale: It connects weight-based structure selection in a general network to learning which logical rules or predicate combinations matter in TensorLogic.

r003.rationale: It does not mention extending propositional rule learning to first-order logic.

r004.rationale: It does not describe choosing which learned structural elements to make explicit and which to keep as weights.
